questions.question: Q: How are young people typically represented in the media?
questions.correctAnswer: Young people are frequently stereotyped negatively — as lazy, rebellious, tech-obsessed, or dangerous. News media often focuses on youth crime, anti-social behaviour, and unemployment. Positive representations (creative, politically engaged, community-active) are less common. This negative bias affects how young people are treated in society.

questions.question: Q: What is the social model of disability and how does it relate to media representation?
questions.correctAnswer: The social model argues that disability is created by society's barriers (physical, attitudinal, institutional) rather than by the impairment itself. In media terms, this means representation can either reinforce barriers (stereotyping disabled people as victims or burdens) or challenge them (showing disabled people as full, complex members of society).

questions.question: Q: Evaluate media representations of social class.
questions.correctAnswer: Working-class people are routinely stereotyped as lazy, uneducated, or criminal — e.g. 'chav' caricatures and benefits-stigma programming. Middle-class life is presented as the norm. This reflects the class background of media producers (predominantly middle-class) and serves commercial interests (sensational stories about 'scroungers' attract audiences). questions.question: Full-Mark Response Evaluate the representation of one marginalised group in media products. Refer to your CSPs. [15 marks] <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Disabled people remain one of the most marginalised groups in media representation, despite constituting 22% of the UK population. They represent approximately 1% of characters on screen, revealing a profound representational gap. When disabled people do appear, they are often confined to stereotypical roles. The 'supercrip' narrative — where a disabled person achieves something remarkable despite their disability — is common but problematic. It positions disability as something to be overcome rather than accepted, and implies that disabled people who don't achieve extraordinary things have somehow failed. The 'victim' representation presents disabled people as objects of pity, reinforcing the medical model that defines them by their impairment. The social model of disability argues that these representations are themselves disabling — they create attitudinal barriers that prevent full social participation. When media repeatedly shows disabled people as helpless or inspirational, it shapes how non-disabled people perceive and interact with disabled people. However, change is happening. Disabled creators on social media (YouTube, TikTok) produce authentic self-representation that challenges mainstream stereotypes. Some TV dramas now feature disabled characters whose disability is incidental rather than defining. The key issue is behind-the-camera representation.
